title: Probability Fundamentals
tagline: Year 2 — Sample spaces, events, and the basic rules of probability

introduction.overview: Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. The sample space lists all possible outcomes. With a few rules (complement, addition, multiplication for independent events) many aptitude problems on coins, dice, cards and bags can be solved.
introduction.placementRelevance: Probability questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with coins, dice, cards or balls in a bag.
introduction.realWorldContext: Weather forecasts, quality control and risk estimates all use probability.

learningObjectives: Write the sample space for coins, dice and cards
Compute the probability of an event as favourable ÷ total
Use the complement rule and the addition rule
Use the multiplication rule for independent events
Handle draws with and without replacement

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Number of ways to choose r items from n: nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). A standard deck has 52 cards: 4 suits of 13, 12 face cards, 4 aces.

coreDefinitions: Experiment: an action with uncertain outcomes (tossing a coin). Sample space S: set of all outcomes.
Event: a subset of the sample space. P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for equally likely outcomes.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). In general P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Probability is relative frequency: if you repeat the experiment many times, the fraction of times the event occurs approaches P(E). Counting favourable and total outcomes carefully is most of the work.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: List the outcomes systematically (a table for two dice, a tree for coins), count the favourable ones, and divide. If the event is "at least one", use the complement.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Addition rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Without replacement
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The second draw has fewer items.

mainNarrative: Define the sample space first. A coin has {H, T}. A die has {1, …, 6}. Two dice have 36 equally likely ordered pairs. A deck has 52 cards. The probability of an event is the count of favourable outcomes divided by the count of all outcomes.
Use the complement for "at least one". Tossing three coins has 8 outcomes; only TTT has no head, so P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.
For "or" questions, use the addition rule and subtract the overlap. In a deck, P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13, because the king of hearts is counted in both groups.
For independent events multiply: two heads in two tosses is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. For draws without replacement, the denominators change: from 5 red and 3 green balls, P(both red) = (5/8) × (4/7) = 5/14.
For dice sums, tabulate the 36 pairs. A sum of 7 occurs in 6 ways, so P = 6/36 = 1/6; a sum of 8 occurs in 5 ways, so P = 5/36.

deepDiveAspects.title: Independent vs mutually exclusive
deepDiveAspects.content: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (probability of both is 0). Independent events do not influence each other. They are different ideas.

deepDiveAspects.title: Combinations in probability
deepDiveAspects.content: When balls are drawn together, use combinations: one white and one black from 4 white and 6 black has 4 × 6 = 24 favourable ways out of C(10, 2) = 45, so P = 8/15.

solvedExamples.title: At least one head
solvedExamples.question: Three coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at least one head.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It is easier to count the single outcome with no head.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Counting favourable outcomes one by one and missing one.

solvedExamples.title: King or heart
solvedExamples.question: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Find the probability that it is a king or a heart.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The king of hearts is in both groups and must be counted once.

solvedExamples.title: Without replacement
solvedExamples.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 green balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second draw has 4 reds among 7 balls.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Use 1 − P(none) for "at least one", a 6 × 6 table for dice sums, and multiply fractions for sequential draws.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating HT and TH as the same.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: A probability must be between 0 and 1; discard options outside.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the sample space before counting.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I list the outcomes of two dice?
